Section 01The question: which expensive calculation can we omit?

A molecular polariton carries a quantum excitation distributed between molecules and a confined radiation field. The atoms still move. Every nuclear configuration changes the molecular excitation energies and transition dipoles, which changes the Hamiltonian seen by the excitation. A direct atomistic calculation can therefore require an electronic-structure calculation on every molecule at every nuclear step, together with excited-state and transition-dipole derivatives to determine the nuclear force.

This paper asks a precise question: can the nuclei move on ground-state trajectories while the electronic–photonic subsystem continues to evolve quantum mechanically? This is the classical path approximation (CPA). It removes backreaction of the excitation on nuclear motion; it does not freeze the molecular Hamiltonian, remove thermal fluctuations, make the photon classical, or eliminate the need to evaluate excitation energies and transition dipoles.

The proposed justification is local dilution of the excited-state force when a single excitation remains spread over many molecules. The paper first compares CPA against the same mean-field Ehrenfest method with its state-dependent nuclear forces retained. It then uses molecular trajectories to construct an atomistic BODIPY–cavity calculation. The logical order matters: agreement with a force-inclusive approximate dynamics method tests the CPA within that method, not exact quantum nuclear dynamics.

These notes derive the force argument, construct the propagation matrices, explain the atomistic workflow, and examine exactly which spatial observable is compared with experiment. Equations below are numbered independently of the paper. “Main” denotes the article; “SI” denotes the supporting information appended after its eight pages in the website PDF.

Source: Main, pp. 1–2; SI, Sec. VII. The tutorial examples and companion code are additional constructions, not new simulations of the published BODIPY data.

Section 03Hilbert spaces and the two uses of a coordinate

For molecule n, let |gn(Rn)⟩ and |en(Rn)⟩ be two electronic states at nuclear configuration Rn. The full matter–photon–nuclear space before approximations is

H=(⨂n=1NHel,n)⊗(⨂α=1MFα)⊗Hnuc.
(1)

Here Fα is the harmonic-oscillator Fock space for cavity mode α. A molecule is truncated to two electronic levels, but the cavity mode is not intrinsically a two-level object. The later single-excitation restriction makes only its zero- and one-photon states relevant.

In the mixed quantum–classical approximation, the nuclear coordinates become classical trajectories. We write |Rn⟩ and |Pn⟩ for real coordinate and momentum columns, with entries in a specified Cartesian or mass-weighted coordinate basis. These Euclidean kets are not electronic wavefunctions. The notation R^nν is reserved for a nuclear position operator before the classical approximation.

In the local electronic basis Bn=(|gn⟩,|en⟩),

[σ^n−]Bn=(0100),[σ^n+]Bn=(0010),[n^n]Bn=(0001).
(2)

An operator with index n is embedded with identities on all other molecular factors. Thus operators on different molecules commute; operators on the same molecule obey the two-state algebra, not harmonic-boson algebra.

Section 04Subtract the common ground energy before propagating

The electronic energy operator of molecule n is

H^el,n(Rn)=Eg(Rn)I^n+ϵn(Rn)n^n,ϵn(Rn)=Ee(Rn)−Eg(Rn).
(3)

Adding the ground energies of all molecules produces a scalar times the identity in the retained electronic–photonic space. It gives a common quantum phase, but its gradient is the ground-state nuclear force. We therefore separate the two uses: retain ∑nEg(Rn) for nuclear propagation and remove it from the quantum matrix.

The quantum matrix then contains ϵn, the vertical electronic gap at the instantaneous geometry. It does not contain the total electronic energy of all molecules. Subtracting this reference improves numerical conditioning and removes a large, physically irrelevant phase from the integrator.

Likewise, the cavity zero-point energy 12∑αEcα may be omitted when the mode frequencies are fixed. Neither subtraction changes quantum populations. Removing a configuration-dependent common energy from the quantum propagation must not be confused with discarding its nuclear derivative.

For an atomistic gap already evaluated as Ee(Rn)−Eg(Rn), do not add a separate reorganization energy simply because a model Hamiltonian writes ϵ0+λ. Those are different parameterizations of the same vertical-versus-relaxed distinction.

Section 05The single-excitation basis and its full matrix

Define the common zero-excitation state |G⟩. Let |En⟩ contain an excited molecule n, all other molecules in their ground state, and no photon. Let |cα⟩ contain one photon in mode α and all molecules in their ground state. Explicitly,

|En⟩=|en⟩⊗⨂m≠n|gm⟩⊗⨂α|0α⟩,|cα⟩=⨂n|gn⟩⊗|1α⟩⊗⨂β≠α|0β⟩.
(4)

In the ordered basis B1=(|E1⟩,…,|EN⟩,|c1⟩,…,|cM⟩), the quantum Hamiltonian is

[H^Q(R)]B1=(E^(R)V^(R)V^†(R)E^c),E^=diag(ϵ1,…,ϵN),E^c=diag(Ec1,…,EcM).
(5)

The hats on the blocks indicate finite-dimensional operators in the stated coordinate bases. The coupling matrix element is Vnα=⟨En|H^Q|cα⟩, an energy. Direct molecule–molecule hopping is absent in the paper's basic model. A Frenkel hopping matrix could be added to E^, but that is an extension, not something already included in the diagonal block.

The quantum state has an (N+M)-component coefficient ket. With loss, its excited-sector norm may decrease; the ground sector must then be reconstructed or propagated separately.

Section 06Spatial phase, polarization, and transition dipole

For a molecule immobilized at center xn, define

Vnα(t)=Eα⟨eα|μeg,n(Rn(t))⟩eikαxn,Eα=ℏωα2ϵVeff.
(6)

Here |eα⟩ is the unit polarization ket in the laboratory Cartesian basis and |μeg,n⟩ is a three-component transition-dipole ket in the same basis. Veff is a mode volume; it is unrelated to the matrix V^. All unit factors must be consistent before multiplying the field amplitude by a dipole.

The phase convention is fixed by the matrix element, not by whether a Fourier exponential looks familiar. Reversing all Fourier signs and relabeling modes consistently gives equivalent physics. Reversing only one of the two off-diagonal blocks breaks Hermiticity.

The paper's model calculation uses a TM-polarization angular factor. Its atomistic dynamics uses a TE polarization whose molecular-frame coordinates are (1,1,1)/3. These are different stated configurations, not interchangeable labels. A coordinate rotation O^ must act on both dipoles and polarization, leaving their dot product unchanged:

⟨eα|μn⟩=⟨eα|O^TO^|μn⟩.
(7)

Source: Main, Eqs. 2–5; SI, Fig. S1 and Eqs. S6–S8.

Section 07Why a multimode cavity is necessary for transport

A single, spatially uniform cavity mode can redistribute population globally but does not by itself define a propagating in-plane dispersion. In the Fabry–Pérot model,

kα=2παNL,Ec(k)=ℏcnrk⊥2+k2,tan⁡θ=kk⊥.
(8)

The lattice spacing is L, the periodic box length is NL, and nr is a refractive index. The SI uses a model with nr=1; retaining nr here makes the convention explicit. The mode spacing depends on the box length, while the largest retained |k| depends on the mode cutoff.

With |x⟩=(x1,…,xN)T in a site-coordinate basis, choose a unitary discrete Fourier transformation

Fαn=e−ikαxnN,|Bα⟩=1N∑neikαxn|En⟩.
(9)

For uniform real coupling amplitude gα in energy units, ⟨Bα|H^Q|cβ⟩=Ngαδαβ. Momentum matching follows from summing the geometric series, not from an additional dynamical approximation. It holds exactly on a complete commensurate lattice with homogeneous energies and couplings.

Section 08A four-molecule Fourier example

Take four molecules at xn=nL, n=0,1,2,3, and retain two photon modes with indices 0 and 1. Write the common single-molecule coupling as g. The molecular-to-photon block and two bright kets are

V^=g(111i1−11−i),|B0⟩=12(1111),|B1⟩=12(1i−1−i).
(10)

The coefficient columns refer to (|E0⟩,…,|E3⟩). Direct multiplication gives V^†|B0⟩=(2g,0)T and V^†|B1⟩=(0,2g)T. The two other Fourier kets lie in the null space of V^†.

This example supplies three useful code tests: bright kets are orthonormal, coupling to the matching mode is Ng, and coupling to the other mode vanishes. An incorrect FFT normalization changes the collective splitting, even when the resulting spectrum still looks qualitatively like an avoided crossing.

For nonuniform molecular energies, the same Fourier transformation remains a valid change of basis. What fails is block diagonality: fluctuations generate off-diagonal couplings between momentum sectors.

Section 09Bright, dark, and polariton projectors

For each homogeneous momentum block,

[H^α](|Bα⟩,|cα⟩)=(ϵ0GαGα∗Ecα),Gα=Ngα.
(11)

Choose the phase so Gα is real and nonnegative. Define δα=Ecα−ϵ0 and Dα=δα2+4Gα2. The eigenenergies and upper-polariton matter probability are

E±,α=ϵ0+Ecα2±Dα2,w+,α=12(1−δαDα),w−,α=1−w+,α.
(12)

These expressions avoid an arctangent quadrant ambiguity. If the cavity lies far above the molecule, the upper polariton is photon-like, so w+→0, a useful limiting check.

The dark projector in the molecular space is

P^D=I^ex−∑α∈K|Bα⟩⟨Bα|.
(13)

The sum above uses orthonormal Fourier bright kets. For general nonorthogonal coupling columns, construct the molecular bright projector from the column space instead:

P^D=I^ex−V^(V^†V^)+V^†,
(14)

where the superscript + denotes the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse, not a polariton branch. Its rank is N−rankV^, equal to N−M only for independent retained columns. With energetic disorder, a vector in the instantaneous null space of V^† need not be an eigenvector of the full Hamiltonian: the molecular block can rotate it into a bright component. “Dark” can therefore mean an optical null space, an ideal reference manifold, or a nearly dark instantaneous eigenstate. State which one is being plotted.

Section 10Deriving the complete mean-field force

Let cn and pα be molecular and photon coefficients of a normalized pure trajectory before loss. The mean-field potential is

U(R)=∑nEg(Rn)+∑n|cn|2ϵn(Rn)+∑α|pα|2Ecα+2Re∑nαcn∗Vnα(Rn)pα.
(15)

To obtain the Ehrenfest force, differentiate at fixed quantum coefficients. The equation of motion already accounts for their change; differentiating the coefficient solution again would not be the mean-field force prescription. With fixed mode frequencies and molecular centers,

|Fn⟩=−|∇nEg⟩−|cn|2|∇nϵn⟩−2Re∑αcn∗pα|∇nVnα⟩.
(16)

The first correction is the excited-minus-ground energy gradient multiplied by local excitation probability. The second is a transition-dipole-gradient force multiplied by a molecular–photon coherence. Neglecting only the first correction is not the full CPA when transition dipoles depend on geometry.

For mobile molecular centers there is also a derivative of eikαxn; the paper fixes the centers, consistent with its immobilized-molecule setting. For a moving electronic basis, derivative couplings introduce further terms. The displayed expression is therefore complete within the particular retained model, not a general all-state molecular force formula.

Source: Main, Eq. 9. The energy functional above is expanded explicitly to explain that equation.

Section 11What CPA changes—and what it leaves intact

The approximation is

ddt|Rn⟩=M^n−1|Pn⟩,ddt|Pn⟩=−|∇nEg(Rn)⟩,iℏddt|ψ⟩=H^Q(R(t))|ψ⟩.
(17)

The mass operator M^n is diagonal in Cartesian mass coordinates; it becomes the identity in a mass-weighted basis. The nuclear equations are independent of |ψ⟩, but the quantum equation is still driven by the evolving nuclear geometry.

This one-way dependence allows two computational stages: generate molecular trajectories, then replay their gaps and dipoles through many cavity calculations. Changing a cavity frequency or loss rate no longer requires repeating the nuclear dynamics within CPA. This reuse is one of the method's most practical advantages.

CPA retains nuclear motion that changes site energies, dipole magnitudes, and dipole directions. It can generate dephasing and population transfer in a polariton basis because the resulting time-dependent Hamiltonians do not generally commute. Nevertheless, prescribed classical fluctuations do not automatically obey the quantum detailed-balance relation of a low-temperature bath. Ground-state thermal sampling alone is not a proof that the coupled quantum subsystem thermalizes correctly.

Section 12Local dilution is not the same as a large molecule count

Let Pex=∑n|cn|2, and define conditional molecular probabilities qn=|cn|2/Pex when Pex>0. The participation number is

Npart=1∑nqn2,∑n|cn|4=Pex2Npart.
(18)

For identical magnitudes f of the local excited-minus-ground force, the squared norm over independent molecular coordinate blocks is

∥δFgap∥2=f2∑n|cn|4=f2Pex2Npart.
(19)

Thus the aggregate Euclidean force norm decreases as Npart−1/2; each equally populated site's correction decreases as Npart−1. These are different statements. The sum of the magnitudes of the local corrections is fPex, which does not vanish. One must not interchange these norms when claiming a thermodynamic limit.

For Pex=0.5 spread evenly over 100 sites, each population is 0.005 and the force norm is 0.05f. For the same molecular population localized on one site, that site's correction is 0.5f. Both states could live inside an ensemble containing a million molecules; the relevant difference is their occupied support.

An ensemble of localized trajectories can have a spatially uniform averaged population. It does not satisfy the per-trajectory delocalization argument. Record maxn|cn|2 and participation along individual trajectories before averaging.

Section 13Bounding the dipole-gradient contribution

A small molecular coefficient is not by itself a bound on a sum over many photon modes. Define a linear map from photon coefficients to the Cartesian dipole-gradient force ket,

D^n|p⟩=∑αpα|∇nVnα⟩.
(20)

Then the triangle and operator-norm inequalities give

∥δFn,μ∥≤2|cn|∥D^n|p⟩∥≤2|cn|∥D^n∥Pph.
(21)

This identifies what must remain controlled as the number of modes grows: the norm of the complete gradient map, not merely each element separately. At fixed collective coupling, a uniform model often has individual couplings proportional to N−1/2, providing further suppression. At fixed single-molecule coupling, increasing the mode count or molecular density is a different limit.

For practical validation, compare selected full-force evaluations with CPA on representative configurations. Use an absolute force scale or a time-averaged ground-force norm. A ratio to the instantaneous ground force is unstable near a ground-state equilibrium point where that force vanishes even though the excitation-induced force is finite.

This is a refinement of the paper's scaling argument, not a replacement for its benchmark evidence. Small neglected forces also have to remain small after accumulation over the propagation time.

Section 14A harmonic model makes backreaction explicit

For one mass-weighted mode per molecule, choose

H^nuc+H^ex−nuc=∑n[P^n22+ωb2Q^n22+(ϵad+λ+CQ^n)n^n],λ=C22ωb2.
(22)

Completing the square in the excited state gives a displaced harmonic well of the same curvature. The force-inclusive and CPA equations are

Q¨nMF+ωb2QnMF=−C|cn(t)|2,Q¨nCPA+ωb2QnCPA=0.
(23)

With equal initial conditions, their coordinate difference satisfies

δQn(t)=−Cωb∫0tsin⁡[ωb(t−s)]|cn(s)|2ds.
(24)

The population history, not only the final population, determines the nuclear error. For a constant population pn, the integral becomes −Cpn[1−cos⁡(ωbt)]/ωb2. The induced gap change is CδQn, hence proportional to pn. This is an explicit mechanism by which local dilution suppresses feedback.

The result also explains two limitations: localized residence can build a substantial displacement, and long-time effects cannot be dismissed solely from an initially delocalized state. For general anharmonic nuclei, this analytic Green-function solution no longer applies, but the force comparison still does.

Section 15Thermal paths and their limitations

For a harmonic coordinate of mass m and frequency ω, thermal Wigner sampling gives independent zero-mean Gaussian variables with variances

⟨Q2⟩W=ℏ2mωcoth⁡βℏω2,⟨P2⟩W=ℏmω2coth⁡βℏω2,⟨QP⟩W=0.
(25)

The ground-state harmonic path is Q(t)=Q(0)cos⁡ωt+P(0)sin⁡ωt/(mω). The resulting classical gap-noise covariance is

⟨CQ(t)CQ(0)⟩W=C2ℏ2mωcoth⁡βℏω2cos⁡ωt.
(26)

This reproduces the symmetrized quantum position correlation of a harmonic oscillator. The unsymmetrized quantum correlation also contains an imaginary commutator part proportional to −isin⁡ωt. CPA classical trajectories do not generate that part merely by Wigner sampling.

The atomistic calculation in this paper instead uses ground-state Langevin molecular dynamics at 300 K. Its nuclear statistics are classical; they are not automatically the harmonic Wigner distribution. The distinction is relevant for high-frequency vibrations and for extrapolations to lower temperatures.

Source: SI, initial conditions and model propagation; SI, atomistic sampling. The variance convention here follows directly from the thermal harmonic oscillator and is used in the teaching checks.

Section 16The electronic basis can itself move

An atomistic electronic basis depends on geometry. Write the matrix of basis kets as U^(t) and the physical wavefunction as |Ψ(t)⟩=U^(t)|c(t)⟩. Differentiating and multiplying by U^† gives

iℏddt|c⟩=[U^†H^U^−iℏU^†U^˙]|c⟩.
(27)

The connection A^=U^†U^˙ is anti-Hermitian for an orthonormal basis, so −iℏA^ is Hermitian. It is distinct from the energy matrix. A basis change cannot be represented only by changing energies while ignoring all overlap information in a general nonadiabatic problem.

The article neglects molecular ground–excited derivative couplings and Born–Oppenheimer corrections, arguing that nonradiative molecular decay is slower than the transport window of interest. This is a separate approximation from omitting excited-state gradients. Near a conical intersection, rapidly changing electronic character or nonradiative decay, one cannot transfer that approximation without checking it.

The single-excitation truncation also excludes states with two molecular excitations. Molecular derivative couplings can connect retained and omitted sectors, so simply adding an arbitrary derivative matrix afterward is not a universally closed extension.

Section 17Why transition-dipole phase alignment is essential

An electronic eigensolver may return |en⟩ or −|en⟩ at adjacent geometries. The excitation energy is unchanged, but the transition dipole changes sign. More generally, under |En′⟩=eiχn|En⟩,

cn′=e−iχncn,Vnα′=e−iχnVnα,H^′=D^†H^D^.
(28)

Here D^ is the diagonal phase transformation on the retained basis. A time-dependent transformation also produces the connection term derived above. A discontinuous dipole sign change with unchanged coefficients is therefore a real, artificial change to the propagated Hamiltonian, not a harmless gauge choice.

For a continuously tracked isolated real electronic state, adjacent wavefunction or transition-density overlaps can set the phase. A signed dipole-overlap heuristic may be useful when that state is isolated and the dipole stays nonzero, but it cannot reliably distinguish a true state crossing or a physical dipole rotation from a solver sign flip. For several nearby electronic states, track the subspace and its overlap matrix.

The SI explicitly states that transition-dipole phases were corrected. A reusable path archive must document this step; a table of absolute dipole magnitudes is not a substitute because it discards orientation and relative phase information.

Section 18The atomistic replay workflow

The calculation naturally separates into a molecular stage and a cavity stage. In the molecular stage, ground-state dynamics produces Rn(tj). Electronic-structure evaluations on those geometries supply ϵn(tj) and the three-component transition dipole. Phase tracking and a common coordinate frame are applied before saving the arrays.

The cavity stage selects molecules or molecular trajectories, positions, photon modes, loss rates, and a prepared quantum state. It constructs H^Q(t), propagates the coefficient ket, and accumulates observables. The same molecular paths may be reused for a controlled comparison of two cavity parameters, which reduces noise in their difference but does not create additional independent samples.

A minimal archive for the companion program contains:

Array Shape Meaning
time_fs (T,) Strictly increasing sample times
gap_eV (T,N) Molecular vertical gaps, not total energies
dipole_projection (T,N) Phase-continuous signed dipole projections divided by one fixed reference dipole
x_nm (N,) Immobilized molecular centers
k_inv_nm (M,) Retained in-plane photon wavevectors
photon_eV (M,) Photon energies
collective_eV (M,) Reference collective coupling energies

The program assumes one common polarization projection for all retained modes. Mode-dependent polarizations require a dipole array or coupling representation with an explicit mode dimension. This is declared rather than silently approximated.

Section 19What the BODIPY electronic-structure calculation actually used

The article calls the workflow ab initio to distinguish geometry-dependent molecular calculations from a fitted harmonic bath. The specific implementation reported here uses semiempirical AM1 ground-state energies and gradients and TDA-AM1 excited-state energies and dipoles, interfaced through SQD and Gaussian. It is not a demonstration of coupled-cluster or high-level multireference accuracy.

The SI describes 540 independent BODIPY trajectories, each 2 ps long at a 1 fs nuclear step and 300 K. The first 1 ps is discarded for equilibration. Groups of 108 molecules provide five realizations for the reported atomistic transport. The propagation uses 51 photon modes and an electronic step of 0.002 fs. The transport cavity energy at normal incidence is about 3.0 eV; the angle-resolved spectral example uses about 2.5 eV to display the avoided crossing clearly.

These numbers serve different roles. A large number of snapshots is not the same as a large number of independent trajectories, because adjacent snapshots are correlated. Five realizations are a reported sampling choice, not a general convergence guarantee. Likewise, the electronic substep resolves the time evolution of an interpolated Hamiltonian; it cannot recover nuclear-frequency content absent from the 1 fs path archive.

Source: SI, Sec. IV; SI, Sec. V. Numerical values above describe this paper's implementation only.

Section 20Time ordering and a stable teaching propagator

For a prescribed trajectory, the exact quantum evolution is the time-ordered exponential

U^(t,0)=Texp⁡[−iℏ∫0tH^Q(s)ds].
(29)

Time ordering is needed because local fluctuations make [H^Q(t),H^Q(s)]≠0. Averaging the energies first and propagating one averaged Hamiltonian generally does not reproduce the ensemble of time-dependent propagations.

A convenient teaching step is the midpoint approximation

|ψ(t+Δt)⟩≈exp⁡[−iH^Q(t+Δt/2)Δt/ℏ]|ψ(t)⟩.
(30)

For a Hermitian midpoint Hamiltonian, the step is exactly norm preserving, although its representation of the time-dependent evolution is only second order. Diagonalize the small midpoint matrix, multiply each eigencomponent by its phase, and transform back. The companion program uses this transparent approach; the article uses RK4 with much smaller electronic substeps.

For large systems, matrix-vector Krylov or Chebyshev propagation avoids dense diagonalization. With homogeneous mode coupling, the off-diagonal action can use FFTs. With a signed site-dependent scalar dipole dn(t), the molecular-to-photon action becomes a Fourier transform of dn∗cn, so a useful factorization can survive certain kinds of dipole disorder. A fully arbitrary Vnα need not have that FFT form.

Section 21Loss: define a rate before writing an exponential

Let κα be a population decay rate in inverse time, and let Wα=ℏκα be its energy width. With L^α=|G⟩⟨cα|,

dρ^dt=−iℏ[H^Q,ρ^]+∑ακα(L^αρ^L^α†−12{L^α†L^α,ρ^}).
(31)

For pure cavity loss, ραα decays as e−καt, a photon–molecule coherence decays at κα/2, and the corresponding amplitude decays as e−καt/2. At normal incidence,

Q=ωcκc=EcWc,τc=1κc=ℏWc.
(32)

For Ec=3.0 eV and Wc=0.010 eV, Q=300 and τc≈65.82 fs. A paper that uses the same symbol for an energy width and a rate requires explicit conversion before implementing its time evolution. This tutorial never puts a quantity in meV directly into an inverse-femtosecond exponential.

Section 22An exact reduced loss construction under CPA

In the absence of pumping and with at most one excitation, a cavity jump goes to the ground state and never returns. For a prescribed molecular path, the excited block satisfies

ρ^˙1=−iℏ(H^effρ^1−ρ^1H^eff†),H^eff=H^Q−iℏ2∑ακα|cα⟩⟨cα|.
(33)

For initially pure excitation, propagate an unnormalized ket |ψ1⟩. Then

ρ^(t)=|ψ1(t)⟩⟨ψ1(t)|+[1−⟨ψ1(t)|ψ1(t)⟩]|G⟩⟨G|.
(34)

This reconstructs the trace-preserving density operator exactly for loss-only relaxation along that fixed path. It is not merely a normalized no-jump prediction. Do not renormalize |ψ1⟩ after each step unless intentionally computing a survival-conditioned observable.

The teaching integrator applies half a damping step, one unitary midpoint step, and another half damping step. A photon amplitude therefore receives e−καΔt/4 in each half-step. This Strang splitting has second-order splitting error when the loss and Hamiltonian do not commute.

This construction relies on the path being independent of jumps. It should not be substituted unchanged into a nonlinear force-feedback ensemble in which different jump histories generate different nuclear trajectories.

Section 23Preparing a localized wavepacket without violating its energy window

A local molecular ket excites a broad energy range and may violate the CPA's initial delocalization condition. The paper instead selects eigenstates within a finite excitation-energy window and combines them to reduce the spatial spread. Let Φ^W contain those eigenkets as columns. Any allowed initial state is

|ψ0⟩=Φ^W|a⟩,⟨a|a⟩=1.
(35)

With P^ex the molecular projector and x^=∑nxn|En⟩⟨En|, define conditional molecular moments

⟨xr⟩ex=⟨a|Φ^W†x^rΦ^W|a⟩⟨a|Φ^W†P^exΦ^W|a⟩,Varex(x)=⟨x2⟩ex−⟨x⟩ex2.
(36)

The SI reports basin-hopping optimization in a selected polariton energy window with ARPACK used to find the relevant eigenstates. This is an optimization procedure, not a unique physical preparation. Its energy bandwidth and resulting spatial participation both matter.

A simpler teaching alternative projects a chosen localized target into the permitted spectral subspace, |ψ0⟩∝P^W|ϕtarget⟩. It obeys the energy window but does not generally minimize the conditional variance. In a periodic box, a coordinate-based width is meaningful only when the packet stays away from the coordinate discontinuity; otherwise use a periodic moment or unwrap the displacement.

Section 24Projected spatial densities are observables, not just labels

For the atomistic simulation, the SI constructs instantaneous eigenspaces P^ξ(t), with ξ representing UP, LP, or dark-like states. The molecular part of a projected wavepacket is

ψξ(xn,t)=⟨En|P^ξ(t)|ψ(t)⟩,pξ,n=|ψξ(xn,t)|2.
(37)

For a density operator, replace this by pξ,n=Tr[ρ^P^ξ|En⟩⟨En|P^ξ]. Each such probability is nonnegative.

However, the sum ∑ξpξ,n need not equal |⟨En|ψ⟩|2. Expanding the latter includes cross terms between distinct projected sectors:

|⟨En|ψ⟩|2=∑ξpξ,n+2Re∑ξ<ζψξ(xn)ψζ(xn)∗.
(38)

Discarding those terms defines a sector-incoherent measurement prescription. The article's atomistic transport distribution specifically uses the sum of UP and dark molecular projected densities, omitting LP and their interference. It is not the full photon-plus-exciton spatial density.

The SI's ideal-model spatial construction also includes photon components in its polariton real-space states. Do not silently equate that definition with the molecular-only atomistic projection. Comparing the methods requires naming the observable used in each case.

Source: SI, Eqs. S19–S24; SI, Eqs. S49–S53.

Section 25Mean-squared displacement, survival, and variance

For any chosen nonnegative weights pn(t), let S(t)=∑npn(t). About a fixed initial center x0, distinguish

M2(t)=∑npn(t)(xn−x0)2,M2|S(t)=M2(t)S(t),VarS(x)=∑npnxn2S−(∑npnxnS)2.
(39)

The first is an unnormalized moment; the second is a survival- or channel-conditioned moment; the third measures width around the current conditional centroid. They agree only under additional conditions. Also, a moment about the initial center at t=0 generally includes the packet's initial width. A change in width may require subtracting that initial value.

Consider two outward-moving peaks at x=±vt with total selected weight S=e−κt. Then

M2(t)=v2t2e−κt,M2|S(t)=v2t2.
(40)

The raw moment reaches a maximum at t=2/κ and then falls, while the surviving packet continues moving outward. Loss alone can therefore make a transient MSD peak. Dark-state deposition and the choice of projected sector provide additional ways to change the measured moment.

The companion script outputs molecular weight, photon weight, total survival, raw molecular moment, and conditional molecular moment separately. None is mislabeled as the paper's UP-plus-dark projected observable.

Section 26Connecting a population profile to differential transmission

The paper models the connection to the transient differential transmission through a weight of the form eηdpn−1. The measured second-moment proxy is

M2,sig(t)=∑n[eηdpn(t)−1](xn−x0)2.
(41)

When maxn|ηdpn|≪1, Taylor expansion gives

M2,sig=ηdM2+(ηd)22∑npn2(xn−x0)2+⋯.
(42)

Thus the leading signal is a scaled unnormalized moment under that measurement model. It is not automatically the variance of a normalized optical image. The paper reports a scale factor ηd=0.0222 for comparison with the cited experiment. That is a stated calibration, not an independently predicted absorption coefficient.

A careful reproduction must specify the instrument response, background subtraction, which polariton sectors are detected, spatial fit procedure, and whether the experimental image is normalized at each time. Matching an apparent MSD curve after applying a scale factor is evidence for a dynamical trend; it is not a unique determination of every microscopic mechanism.

Source: Main, Eq. 14 and discussion of Fig. 3.

Section 27What a photon-weighted spectral calculation measures

For frozen geometry R and a chosen cavity momentum, the source diagonalizes an independent single-mode Hamiltonian. A photon-weighted spectral density is

Aph(E,k)=⟨∑J|⟨ck|ΦJ(R,k)⟩|2δ[E−EJ(R,k)]⟩R.
(43)

The sum rule is ∫dEAph(E,k)=1 for one retained photon basis state and a complete eigenbasis. Replacing the delta function by a normalized Gaussian preserves this rule. The SI reports Gaussian broadening of about 26 meV and averaging over molecular snapshots.

This construction captures where photon-like eigenstates occur. A fully specified experimental transmission coefficient also depends on coupling to input/output ports, losses, optical geometry, and interference. Treating the photon-weighted density of states as a transmission model is therefore an explicit modeling step.

For a homogeneous translationally symmetric ensemble, momentum blocks decouple and a mode-resolved construction is natural. A single disordered snapshot can mix different momentum sectors. A single-mode calculation should not be asserted equivalent to the full multimode realization without checking the symmetry or ensemble approximation being used.

Section 28Coarse graining the molecular lattice

The atomistic simulation uses 108 molecules separated by 1500 Å. The SI compares this with an estimated physical spacing of 40 Å and introduces a scale factor s=37.5. Its proposed transformation is

N~=N/s,L~=sL,g~=sg,N~L~=NL,N~g~=Ng.
(44)

The box length and low-momentum mode spacing are preserved, and the ideal collective splitting can be preserved. The maximum molecular Fourier momentum is reduced, and the number of dark states changes. These latter changes are physical changes to the finite model, not merely relabeling of coordinates.

In particular, N−M changes from a large reservoir to a number comparable to M in the atomistic example. Dark-to-bright return, entropy, local population fluctuations, and force dilution can consequently change even when the ideal polariton dispersion is unchanged. Preserving the dispersion is necessary for a controlled low-momentum comparison, but not sufficient to preserve all relaxation dynamics.

For N~=108, L~=150 nm, the simulated box is 16.2 µm. Its corresponding N=sN~ at 4 nm spacing is 4050, not the 10001-site model benchmark. These are separate parameter sets. A reproducibility table should keep them separate rather than merging all numbers into one “system size.”

Source: SI, scaling argument in Sec. V. The cautions follow from the changed rank and state counts.

Section 29Reading the figures as controlled comparisons

Figure 1 compares force-inclusive and CPA model simulations using group velocities, transient moments, and polariton/dark/ground populations. Figure 2 compares spatial profiles and checks that site populations remain small. These two figures jointly support the proposed approximation more directly than a comparison of a single integrated moment would.

Figure 3 changes the level of molecular description: geometry-dependent BODIPY gaps and dipoles enter the model, and the resulting spectra and transport trends are compared with experiment. Figure 4 varies coupling and cavity loss. A change between these figures is not purely a change of nuclear-force approximation; molecular electronic structure, sample size, spacing, and spectral preparation also differ.

A useful reproduction starts with a paired force-inclusive/CPA calculation using identical initial conditions and all other parameters held fixed. Only after that comparison is controlled should one change the molecular electronic-structure model. For a cavity-loss calculation, also compare a directly reconstructed trace and the sum of all reported state populations.

The source's main text gives 141 cavity modes for the model benchmark, whereas SI S6 gives 283. The notes do not choose one silently. Resolve the production input before claiming an exact numerical reproduction. The same care applies to the model reorganization-energy convention discussed below.

Section 30A numerical explorer for scales and observable definitions

The calculator evaluates an ideal one-block polariton, a uniform delocalized force estimate, and the two-peak loss example. It is not a molecular dynamics simulation. Its population input is the total molecular fraction of a normalized state, distributed uniformly over the specified participating sites.

The force-norm entry is measured relative to the same single-site gradient magnitude, not relative to a ground-state force that might be zero. The two-peak attenuation rate is deliberately taken to be the bare cavity rate; a real mixed polariton has composition-dependent decay and relaxation, so that curve should not be identified with a fitted polariton lifetime.

Section 31The companion program and an actual replay input

Download the NumPy teaching program

The script assembles the molecular–photon matrix, propagates signed gap/dipole time series, and reconstructs lost population in the ground state. Its demonstrations use explicitly labeled synthetic harmonic fluctuations, not AM1 output. A small fixed-path density-matrix reference tests the loss block, and a force finite-difference check verifies the mean-field expression.

python cpa_transport_teaching.py --test
python cpa_transport_teaching.py --demo --output cpa_demo.csv
python cpa_transport_teaching.py --replay molecular_paths.npz --output replay.csv

The input layout is defined in the replay-workflow section and the script's docstring. The replay mode is meant for a modest test system: it uses dense midpoint diagonalization and does not replace the production RK4/FFT or electronic-structure workflow. The script never calls Gaussian or downloads molecular data.

There is an important sampling distinction: averaging densities from independently propagated paths is correct; averaging coefficient kets and then squaring is generally not. The latter introduces interference between separate classical realizations that were meant to be an incoherent ensemble.

Section 32Conventions that prevent implementation errors

The main article and SI use several overlapping notations. The following checks remove ambiguity before a calculation starts.

Schrödinger sign. Main Eq. 7 and SI S48 use iℏψ˙=H^ψ. The opposite sign printed in SI S26 is not used here. The short-time step must approach I^−iH^Δt/ℏ.

Reorganization energy. For 12ω2Q2+CQ, completing the square lowers the minimum by C2/(2ω2). The SI spectral-density/reorganization equations contain a factor-of-two inconsistency under this convention. Report the physical displacement and chosen spectral normalization rather than transferring the symbol λ alone.

Loss amplitude. Starting from the Lindblad generator gives an amplitude factor e−κΔt/2 and a population factor e−κΔt. The SI's printed stochastic factors should be checked against this identity before implementation.

Variance. The conditional variance is ∑nqnxn2−(∑nqnxn)2, not ∑nqnxn2−∑n(qnxn)2. This distinction matters in interpreting SI S37.

Thermal sampling. Position and momentum variances carry different powers of mass and frequency. The variance formulas given above are the directly checkable implementation convention. These clarifications change neither the stated physical hypothesis nor the distinction between benchmark and atomistic calculations.

Section 33Validity, error budgets, and what is not established

CPA is most defensible for low excitation density, spatially extended trajectories, bounded dipole gradients, and observables on timescales short enough that neglected feedback does not accumulate strongly. Local photoisomerization, bond breaking, trapping, or a highly localized initial excitation may require excited-state forces even inside a very large cavity ensemble.

For many excitations, the relevant local occupation can scale as Nexc/Npart. A large total molecule count no longer guarantees a small local force. Likewise, a small coefficient in a decayed, unnormalized ket does not prove that the surviving excitation is delocalized. Monitor both survival and conditional participation.

A layered error budget separates the electronic-structure approximation, nuclear classical treatment, omission of derivative couplings, CPA backreaction, finite excitation manifold, mode cutoff, coarse graining, trajectory sampling, temporal interpolation, propagation step, and observation model. Reducing the electronic timestep only addresses one of these.

The paper gives encouraging direct comparisons in the regime tested. It does not prove uniform accuracy for every molecular polariton, every dark state, arbitrary excitation density, or arbitrary reaction coordinate. The main benefit of the force derivation is that it tells us what to monitor when leaving that regime.

Section 34Exercises with worked solutions

1. Count states for 108 molecules and 51 photon modes.

The single-excitation block has 159 basis kets. Including the zero-excitation state for loss gives 160. For independent homogeneous coupling columns, there are 51 UP states, 51 LP states, and 57 dark molecular states. The sum 51 + 51 + 57 = 159 checks the count.

2. Differentiate one coupling term in the mean-field energy.

A Hermitian pair contributes cn∗Vnαpα+pα∗Vnα∗cn=2Re(cn∗Vnαpα). At fixed coefficients its negative gradient is −2Re[cn∗pα|∇nVnα⟩]. Both members of the pair are necessary for a real force.

3. Compare local and aggregate force scaling.

With total molecular population 0.4 spread over 400 sites, every site has population 0.001. Each correction is 0.001 times a common gradient magnitude. The Euclidean norm over 400 independent equal-gradient coordinate blocks is 0.4/400=0.02 times that magnitude, while the sum of magnitudes is 0.4 times it.

4. Can a uniform ensemble average justify CPA?

No. Consider an ensemble in which each trajectory is entirely localized on a different randomly chosen molecule. The averaged population is uniform, but every trajectory has maximum population one and participation one. The neglected force is large on the occupied molecule in each trajectory.

5. Derive the constant-population nuclear displacement.

Integrating the harmonic response kernel for constant population p gives δQ=−Cp(1−cos⁡ωbt)/ωb2. At half a vibrational period the displacement is −2Cp/ωb2. The same finite displacement grows linearly with local occupation even when the total ensemble is large.

6. Check a transition-dipole phase flip.

For a real sign flip on one molecular ket, multiply its coefficient by −1 and its entire coupling row by −1. The Hamiltonians are related by a diagonal unitary similarity transformation and all physical probabilities agree. Changing only the dipole row while leaving the evolving coefficient unchanged is not the same representation of the original dynamics.

7. Convert a 20 meV cavity width into lifetime and Q.

With ℏ=658.2119569 meV fs, τc=32.9106 fs. At 3 eV, Q=3000/20=150. The amplitude lifetime is twice the population lifetime for an isolated damped photon, so it is important to name which one is being reported.

8. Verify the reconstructed trace after cavity loss.

If the excited-sector norm is 0.63, assign ground-state probability 0.37. The full density operator then has trace one and nonnegative eigenvalues. Renormalizing the excited ket to norm one would discard the survival probability and yield a conditional state instead.

9. Find the peak of the attenuated ballistic moment.

Differentiating v2t2e−κt gives v2e−κt(2t−κt2). The nonzero maximum is at 2/κ. The normalized moment remains v2t2, so the raw peak is not evidence of a reversal of propagation.

10. Show why projected branch densities need not sum to a local population.

At resonance in a one-molecule cavity, |E⟩=(|+⟩−|−⟩)/2 for a suitable phase choice. The molecular amplitudes of the two projected pieces have squared magnitudes 1/4 and 1/4, while the full molecular probability is one. The missing half comes from their interference.

11. What survives the lattice rescaling by s?

The transformations preserve box length, low-k spacing, and the ideal collective coupling. They do not preserve the number of dark states, full molecular Brillouin zone, or the local force per occupied site. Those changes require independent convergence checks.

12. Check the conditional variance for two equally weighted sites.

At positions −a and +a, each conditional probability is 1/2. The centroid is zero and the variance is a2. The incorrect sum of squared weighted coordinates gives a2/2, immediately revealing the error.

13. Does a smaller electronic step improve nuclear sampling?

It improves integration of the Hamiltonian supplied to the propagator. It cannot restore fast molecular fluctuations removed by a coarse nuclear sampling interval. Converge path resolution and quantum integration separately.

14. Why should densities, rather than trajectory amplitudes, be averaged?

Independent nuclear realizations represent an incoherent ensemble ρ^=∑rwr|ψr⟩⟨ψr|. Squaring ∑rwr|ψr⟩ adds inter-realization cross terms and is not this density operator. The distinction persists even when each trajectory has perfectly coherent quantum dynamics.

Section 35Sources, related notes, and a practical reading order

The primary source is B. X. K. Chng, B. M. Weight, M. E. Mondal, and P. Huo, Ab Initio Polariton Transport Dynamics with the Classical Path Approximation, Nano Letters 26, 6055–6062 (2026), DOI 10.1021/acs.nanolett.6c00383. The website's combined article and SI supplies all source sections cited here. SI pages S1–S23 correspond to PDF pages 9–31.

For background, read the 2025 polariton transport tutorial for Fourier propagation and ideal dispersions, the 2025 linear-spectroscopy methods tutorial for matrix-free propagation, and the 2024 adiabaticity tutorial for moving eigenbases and phase conventions. The collective-effects review tutorial explains why local dilution, dark-state multiplicity, and global collective effects can coexist.

The explicit matrices, bounds, measurement-operator interpretation, and teaching program are tutorial additions. They expose assumptions needed to translate the paper into a working calculation and should not be mistaken for additional published numerical results.
